title: Autacoids: Histamine, Serotonin & Eicosanoids
summary: Local mediators and the drugs that mimic or block them.

lessons.title: Histamine and Antihistamines

levels.kid:
Your body has tiny alarm cells called **mast cells**. When they think something bad got in, like pollen or a bee sting, they spill out a chemical called **histamine**.

Histamine is like a fire alarm. It makes your nose run, your eyes itch, your skin get red bumps, and your sneezes go "achoo!" That is your body trying to wash the bad stuff out.

But sometimes the alarm rings when there is no real danger. That is an **allergy**.

**Antihistamines** are medicines that cover the alarm's buttons so histamine can't push them. Some old ones also make you very sleepy. Newer ones mostly don't.

For a really big allergy emergency, doctors use a different medicine first: **epinephrine**.
levels.hs:
**Histamine** is made from the amino acid histidine and stored mainly in **mast cells** and basophils. It is also made in the stomach lining and by brain neurons that keep you awake.

It acts on four receptors:
- **H1**: itching, sneezing, runny nose, hives, airway tightening, leaky blood vessels.
- **H2**: tells stomach cells to make **acid**.
- **H3**: a brake on histamine release in the brain.
- **H4**: on immune cells.

**H1 antihistamines** treat allergies, hives and itch.
- **First generation** (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine, promethazine): enter the brain, so they cause **drowsiness**. They also block muscarinic receptors: dry mouth, constipation, trouble peeing. Some help **motion sickness** (meclizine, dimenhydrinate).
- **Second generation** (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine): barely enter the brain, so far less sleepiness.

**H2 blockers** (famotidine, cimetidine) lower stomach acid for heartburn and ulcers.

Important: in **anaphylaxis**, the life-saving drug is **epinephrine**. Antihistamines only help the itch and hives; they cannot reopen a closing airway or raise a crashing blood pressure fast enough.
levels.college:
**Synthesis and storage.** Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine, which is stored with heparin in mast-cell and basophil granules, released by IgE cross-linking, complement anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a), and directly by some drugs (morphine, vancomycin, radiocontrast). Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric fundus and neurons of the hypothalamic **tuberomammillary nucleus** are non-mast-cell sources. Histamine is inactivated by diamine oxidase and histamine N-methyltransferase.

**Receptors.**
- **H1** (Gq → PLC → IP3/Ca2+): bronchial and gut smooth muscle contraction; endothelial NO and prostacyclin release → vasodilation; endothelial contraction → increased permeability (wheal); sensory nerve activation (itch). Together these form the Lewis triple response: red spot, flare, wheal.
- **H2** (Gs → cAMP): parietal cell acid secretion; positive chronotropy.
- **H3** (Gi/o): presynaptic auto- and heteroreceptor in the CNS.
- **H4** (Gi): eosinophil, mast cell and T-cell chemotaxis.

**H1 antihistamines are inverse agonists**, stabilizing the inactive receptor state. First-generation agents are lipophilic, cross the blood–brain barrier and block muscarinic, α1 and sometimes 5-HT receptors. Second-generation agents are more polar or zwitterionic and are **P-glycoprotein substrates**, so they are pumped out of the brain.

**Withdrawn lesson:** terfenadine and astemizole blocked cardiac **hERG** potassium channels, prolonging QT and causing torsades when CYP3A4 inhibitors raised their levels. **Fexofenadine**, terfenadine's active metabolite, kept the antihistamine effect without the hERG problem.

**H2 antagonists**: cimetidine inhibits several CYPs and has antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia); famotidine has neither problem. Ranitidine was withdrawn in 2020 because of NDMA contamination, a manufacturing and stability issue rather than a receptor effect.

**H3**: **pitolisant**, an H3 inverse agonist, increases histamine release and treats narcolepsy.
levels.phd:
**Constitutive activity and inverse agonism.** H1 receptors signal measurably without agonist, and essentially every clinically used "antagonist" reduces this basal activity. This explains why antihistamines work best prophylactically: they shift the receptor population toward the inactive state before a histamine surge, rather than racing it for occupancy. Constitutive H1 signaling also drives NF-κB activity, offering one route for modest anti-inflammatory effects independent of histamine.

**Brain histamine.** The tuberomammillary neurons project across the cortex and fire tonically during wakefulness, falling silent in sleep, under GABAergic inhibition from the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus. Sedation by first-generation antihistamines is therefore a direct readout of central H1 occupancy, and PET studies with radiolabeled doxepin quantify it: high brain H1 occupancy correlates with impaired psychomotor performance, even when patients do not feel sleepy. Orexin neurons excite tuberomammillary neurons, which links narcolepsy biology to the rationale for pitolisant: blocking the H3 autoreceptor's constitutive brake raises histamine tone.

**Blood–brain barrier pharmacokinetics.** Second-generation selectivity is a transport phenomenon. Cetirizine (the carboxylic acid metabolite of hydroxyzine) and fexofenadine are zwitterions with low passive permeability and active efflux by P-glycoprotein. Cetirizine still produces measurable sedation in a minority, consistent with its partial brain occupancy.

**Selectivity as structure.** Many first-generation antihistamines share the ethylamine pharmacophore with tricyclic antidepressants and phenothiazines; promethazine is literally a phenothiazine. This explains the class's antimuscarinic, antiadrenergic and sodium-channel-blocking effects and why diphenhydramine in overdose behaves like a tricyclic, with QRS widening.

**H4** couples to Gi and mediates eosinophil and mast-cell chemotaxis and pruritus that H1 blockers incompletely suppress, which is why H4 antagonists have been investigated for atopic itch.
levels.expert:
**Anaphylaxis order of operations.** Epinephrine intramuscularly into the lateral thigh is first-line and is never delayed for an antihistamine. Epinephrine's α1 effects reverse vasodilation and mucosal edema, β2 effects open bronchi, and β2-mediated cAMP stabilizes mast cells. H1 and H2 blockers are adjuncts for skin and itch; glucocorticoids do not treat the acute event. A serum **tryptase** drawn early supports the diagnosis afterward. Patients on β-blockers may respond poorly to epinephrine; glucagon bypasses the receptor.

**Drug-induced histamine release** is not IgE-mediated. Rapid **vancomycin** infusion causes flushing and hypotension (infusion reaction); slowing the infusion and pretreating with antihistamines usually allows continuation. Morphine and meperidine release histamine; fentanyl does not, which is one reason it is preferred in hemodynamically fragile patients.

**First-generation hazards in practice.**
- Older adults: diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine are on the Beers list because antimuscarinic load causes delirium, urinary retention and falls. A delirious postoperative neurosurgical patient deserves a medication review before a CT.
- Children: paradoxical excitation; promethazine carries a boxed warning against use under age two because of fatal respiratory depression.
- Promethazine injection: extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes severe tissue injury and gangrene; many hospitals restrict the injectable form.
- Overdose: anticholinergic toxidrome (hot, dry, flushed, mydriatic, delirious, retaining urine), seizures and sodium-channel blockade with wide QRS, treated with sodium bicarbonate. Physostigmine is considered only for pure anticholinergic delirium with a narrow QRS, with toxicology input.

**H2 blockers in the ICU**: famotidine for stress-ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated or coagulopathic patients, including after brain injury, where Cushing ulcers occur. Cimetidine's CYP inhibition can raise levels of phenytoin and warfarin, which matters on a neurosurgical service.

**Scombroid**: flushing and headache after spoiled fish is histamine poisoning, not fish allergy, and responds to antihistamines.

keyPoints: Histamine: mast cells/basophils, gastric ECL cells, tuberomammillary neurons (wakefulness)

Terfenadine/astemizole withdrawn for hERG QT prolongation; fexofenadine is the safe active metabolite
Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine first; antihistamines are adjuncts
Pitolisant = H3 inverse agonist for narcolepsy; cimetidine inhibits CYPs and is antiandrogenic

examples.tr: Tricyclic-like sodium-channel blockade; treat with sodium bicarbonate
Direct mast-cell histamine release, not allergy; slow the infusion

test.q: Which histamine receptor mainly drives gastric acid secretion?
test.explain: H2 (Gs → cAMP) on parietal cells stimulates acid secretion.

test.q: Why do second-generation antihistamines cause less drowsiness?
choices: They block H2 instead of H1 receptors, leaving brain histamine signaling intact
They are pumped out of the brain by P-glycoprotein and cross the blood–brain barrier poorly
They are full agonists at H1, so they activate wake-promoting neurons instead
They are given by injection, so too little reaches the brain to sedate
test.explain: Polarity and P-gp efflux keep brain H1 occupancy low.

test.q: Terfenadine was withdrawn because it:
choices: Blocked cardiac hERG channels, prolonging QT
test.explain: With CYP3A4 inhibitors, parent terfenadine accumulated and caused torsades.

test.q: The first-line drug for anaphylaxis is:
test.explain: Only epinephrine reverses vasodilation, airway edema and bronchospasm fast enough.

test.q: Which side effect is typical of first-generation but not second-generation H1 blockers?
test.explain: First-generation agents block muscarinic receptors.

test.q: Cimetidine differs from famotidine because cimetidine:
choices: Is an irreversible proton pump inhibitor
Inhibits CYP enzymes and has antiandrogenic effects
Lowers acid by blocking gastrin receptors
test.explain: Cimetidine's imidazole ring binds CYPs; it can cause gynecomastia.

test.q: Pitolisant treats narcolepsy by acting at which receptor?
test.explain: Blocking the H3 autoreceptor brake increases brain histamine release, promoting wakefulness.

test.q: Which drug is useful for motion sickness?
test.explain: Central H1 and muscarinic blockade in vestibular pathways.

test.q: Fentanyl is sometimes preferred over morphine in unstable patients partly because fentanyl:
choices: Does not cause significant histamine release
Raises blood pressure through α1 agonism
test.explain: Morphine releases histamine, causing vasodilation and hypotension.

test.q: Name the enzyme that makes histamine from histidine.
test.explain: Histidine decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group from histidine.

test.q: Brain histamine neurons that keep you awake sit in the ___ nucleus of the hypothalamus.
test.explain: Tuberomammillary neurons fire during wakefulness.

test.q: What mast-cell enzyme is measured in blood to confirm anaphylaxis afterward?
test.explain: Tryptase is released with histamine but persists longer in blood.

test.q: Clinically used H1 "antagonists" are actually ___ agonists, reducing the receptor's constitutive activity.
test.explain: They stabilize the inactive receptor conformation.

kidTest.q: Which cells spill out histamine?
kidTest.explain: Mast cells are the body's histamine alarm cells.

kidTest.q: Histamine can make your nose:
kidTest.explain: Histamine makes a runny nose and sneezing.

kidTest.q: What do antihistamines do?
choices: Stop histamine from pushing its buttons
Make lots more histamine inside your body
Sweep the pollen off flowers outside
Turn off your heart so it can take a nap
kidTest.explain: They cover the receptor buttons.

kidTest.q: An allergy is when your body's alarm:
choices: Never works, even in a fire
Rings when there is no real danger
kidTest.explain: The immune system overreacts to harmless things.

kidTest.q: For a huge allergy emergency, doctors first use:
kidTest.explain: Epinephrine saves lives in anaphylaxis.

kidTest.q: Old antihistamines often make you feel ___.
kidTest.explain: They get into the brain, where histamine keeps you awake.

advancedTest.q: A patient overdoses on diphenhydramine and has a wide QRS. The mechanism and first treatment are:
choices: hERG potassium-channel blockade; intravenous magnesium sulfate
advancedTest.explain: Diphenhydramine has tricyclic-like sodium-channel blocking effects; bicarbonate raises sodium load and pH.

advancedTest.q: PET studies of first-generation antihistamines show that psychomotor impairment correlates best with:
choices: Plasma histamine concentration measured at the same time
Gastric pH, reflecting H2 receptor blockade in the stomach
Peripheral wheal-and-flare size after a histamine skin prick
Brain H1 receptor occupancy, even without subjective sleepiness
advancedTest.explain: Subjective sleepiness underestimates impairment.

advancedTest.q: A patient on a nonselective β-blocker has anaphylaxis refractory to epinephrine. A logical add-on is:
advancedTest.explain: Glucagon raises cAMP through its own receptor, bypassing β-blockade.

advancedTest.q: Why is fexofenadine free of terfenadine's cardiac risk?
choices: It is converted back to terfenadine mainly during gut absorption
It is an H2 blocker, so it has no effect on cardiac H1 or hERG
It inhibits CYP3A4, preventing buildup of cardiac metabolites
It is the carboxylic acid metabolite, which does not meaningfully block hERG
advancedTest.explain: The parent drug, not the metabolite, blocked hERG.

lessons.title: Serotonin Receptors and Drugs

levels.kid:
**Serotonin** is a messenger chemical. Most of it is not in your brain at all. It is in your **tummy**, where it helps your gut squeeze food along.

In the brain, serotonin helps with mood, sleep and feeling full.

Serotonin has lots of different "locks" it can open, called **receptors**. There are more than a dozen! Different medicines are keys that fit only some locks:
- One kind of medicine blocks the lock that makes you throw up, so it stops sick tummies.
- Another kind keeps more serotonin around in the brain to help with sadness.

Too much serotonin all at once is dangerous. A person can get very hot, shaky and jumpy. Doctors call that **serotonin syndrome** and treat it fast.
levels.hs:
**Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT)** is made from the amino acid **tryptophan**. About 90% of the body's serotonin is in the gut, made by enterochromaffin cells. Platelets soak it up from blood and release it when they clump. In the brain it comes from the **raphe nuclei** in the brainstem.

It is broken down by **monoamine oxidase (MAO)** into 5-HIAA, which is measured in urine to diagnose **carcinoid tumors** that pour out serotonin.

Receptor families and drug examples:
- **5-HT1A**: buspirone (anxiety).
- **5-HT1B/1D**: triptans (migraine).
- **5-HT2A**: blocked by atypical antipsychotics.
- **5-HT3**: the only ion-channel serotonin receptor; **ondansetron** blocks it to stop vomiting.
- **5-HT4**: speeds gut movement (prucalopride for constipation).

**SSRIs** (fluoxetine, sertraline) block the serotonin transporter (**SERT**), keeping serotonin in the synapse.

**Serotonin syndrome** happens when several serotonergic drugs combine (for example an SSRI plus tramadol, linezolid or an MAO inhibitor). Signs: agitation, fever, sweating, diarrhea, and **clonus** (rhythmic jerking reflexes), especially in the legs. Treatment: stop the drugs, cool, sedate with benzodiazepines, and sometimes cyproheptadine.
levels.college:
**Synthesis.** Tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) is rate-limiting: **TPH1** in gut enterochromaffin cells and the pineal gland, **TPH2** in raphe neurons. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts 5-HTP to 5-HT. Serotonin is packaged by VMAT2, cleared by **SERT**, and degraded by **MAO-A** to 5-HIAA. The pineal gland converts it to melatonin. Platelets lack TPH but accumulate 5-HT through SERT.

**Receptors** (seven families, at least 14 subtypes):
- **5-HT1** (Gi/o): 1A somatodendritic autoreceptor on raphe neurons and postsynaptic in hippocampus (buspirone, vilazodone and vortioxetine have partial agonism); 1B/1D on cranial vessels and trigeminal terminals (triptans); 1F neuronal (lasmiditan).
- **5-HT2** (Gq): 2A cortical and platelet (blocked by atypical antipsychotics; pimavanserin is an inverse agonist for Parkinson disease psychosis); 2B on heart valves (agonism causes valvulopathy: fenfluramine, pergolide); 2C appetite (lorcaserin, withdrawn in 2020 after a cancer signal).
- **5-HT3**: pentameric ligand-gated cation channel on vagal afferents and the area postrema/chemoreceptor trigger zone. Antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, palonosetron) treat chemotherapy and postoperative nausea.
- **5-HT4** (Gs): enteric neurons; prucalopride (selective), cisapride (withdrawn for hERG).
- **5-HT5, 6, 7**: CNS; 5-HT7 affinity contributes to some antipsychotics and vortioxetine.

**Serotonin syndrome** is a dose-related toxidrome (not idiosyncratic). **Hunter criteria** center on clonus (spontaneous, inducible or ocular), agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia and hypertonia with fever. Key culprits beyond SSRIs/SNRIs: MAOIs, linezolid and **methylene blue** (both MAO inhibitors), tramadol, meperidine, fentanyl. **Cyproheptadine** (5-HT2A antagonist) is the usual antidote.

**Carcinoid syndrome** (usually with liver metastases): flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valve fibrosis. Somatostatin analogs reduce secretion; **telotristat ethyl** inhibits TPH to control diarrhea.
levels.phd:
**Why 90% in the gut matters.** Peripheral and central serotonin pools are separate because 5-HT does not cross the blood–brain barrier. Gut-derived 5-HT regulates motility, secretion, platelet function and even bone formation, which is why TPH1-selective inhibition (telotristat) can treat carcinoid diarrhea without psychiatric effects.

**Autoreceptor dynamics and the antidepressant delay.** Acute SSRI exposure raises extracellular 5-HT most in the raphe, activating somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors, which reduce firing and blunt terminal release. Over weeks, autoreceptor desensitization permits sustained terminal 5-HT elevation. This model (Blier and de Montigny) motivated pindolol augmentation trials and drugs combining SERT inhibition with 5-HT1A partial agonism. It is incomplete: neurotrophic and plasticity effects (BDNF–TrkB signaling) likely contribute too.

**Biased signaling at 5-HT2A.** Agonists can stabilize distinct conformations that preferentially recruit Gq versus β-arrestin pathways. Structural work suggests that some ligands engage Gq-linked signaling linked to cortical plasticity, an active area of drug design for depression.

**The 5-HT2B safety lesson.** Valvular interstitial cells express 5-HT2B; sustained agonism drives mitogenic signaling and fibrotic plaques. Fenfluramine's metabolite norfenfluramine, pergolide and high-dose cabergoline are agonists here. Screening new compounds for 5-HT2B agonism is now routine in safety pharmacology.

**5-HT3 receptor pharmacology.** As a Cys-loop channel, it desensitizes rapidly. Palonosetron has higher affinity and a long half-life and may induce receptor internalization and inhibit crosstalk with NK1 signaling, which may explain its delayed-phase antiemetic efficacy.

**Serotonin toxicity as a spectrum.** Isbister and Whyte argued that "syndrome" understates its concentration dependence: severity tracks the increase in intrasynaptic 5-HT, and life-threatening cases nearly always involve an MAO inhibitor plus a serotonin reuptake inhibitor or releaser.
levels.expert:
**Distinguishing hyperthermic rigid toxidromes** at the bedside:
- **Serotonin toxicity**: onset within hours of a new or increased drug; hyperreflexia and **clonus**, worse in the legs; mydriasis; diarrhea; agitation.
- **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome**: days to evolve after a dopamine antagonist or withdrawal of a dopamine agonist; **lead-pipe rigidity**, bradyreflexia, very high CK.
- **Anticholinergic toxicity**: dry, hot skin, absent bowel sounds, normal reflexes.
- **Malignant hyperthermia**: in the operating room after volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine; rising end-tidal CO2; dantrolene.
In serotonin toxicity, antipyretics do not work because the heat is muscular. Severe cases need sedation, paralysis and intubation; physical restraints worsen hyperthermia.

**Operating-room traps.**
- **Methylene blue** (for vasoplegia, methemoglobinemia or parathyroid localization) is a potent MAO-A inhibitor. In a patient on an SSRI it has caused serious serotonin toxicity.
- **Linezolid** for a postoperative shunt or wound infection in a patient on an SSRI needs a monitoring plan or an alternative.
- **Fentanyl, tramadol and meperidine** add serotonergic load; meperidine with an MAOI is a classic fatal combination.

**Ondansetron** is a workhorse for postoperative nausea after craniotomy, where retching raises intracranial pressure. Watch QT prolongation with other QT drugs and electrolyte derangement, and remember constipation.

**SSRIs and bleeding.** Platelets cannot synthesize 5-HT, so SERT blockade depletes platelet serotonin and weakens aggregation. The absolute risk is small, but it adds to antiplatelets and anticoagulants. For elective spine surgery, many surgeons note it rather than stop the SSRI, because abrupt discontinuation causes a withdrawal syndrome and relapse risk.

**Carcinoid crisis**: tumor manipulation or anesthesia can trigger flushing, bronchospasm and hemodynamic collapse; octreotide is given before and during surgery.

keyPoints: 5-HT from tryptophan (TPH rate-limiting: TPH1 gut/pineal, TPH2 brain); ~90% in gut; degraded by MAO-A to 5-HIAA
5-HT3 is the only ion-channel serotonin receptor; ondansetron/granisetron/palonosetron are antiemetics
5-HT1A buspirone; 1B/1D triptans; 1F lasmiditan; 2A antipsychotics and pimavanserin; 4 prucalopride
5-HT2B agonism → cardiac valvulopathy (fenfluramine, pergolide)
Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia; MAOI combos worst; linezolid and methylene blue inhibit MAO; cyproheptadine
SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin → modest bleeding risk

examples.src: SSRI patient given methylene blue during surgery
Urine 5-HIAA elevated with flushing and diarrhea
examples.tr: Carcinoid syndrome, usually with liver metastases

test.q: Which serotonin receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel?
test.explain: All other 5-HT receptors are GPCRs.

test.q: Ondansetron prevents vomiting by:
choices: Blocking dopamine D2 receptors selectively, in the area postrema and stomach
Blocking 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Activating 5-HT4 receptors in the gut to speed gastric emptying
Inhibiting MAO so serotonin levels fall in the brainstem
test.explain: 5-HT3 antagonism blocks the emetic reflex.

test.q: Where is most of the body's serotonin?
test.explain: About 90% is in the gut.

test.q: The serotonin metabolite measured in urine to diagnose carcinoid tumors is:
test.explain: MAO converts 5-HT to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

test.q: Which finding most strongly points to serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
test.explain: Clonus is central to the Hunter criteria.

test.q: Which antibiotic is an MAO inhibitor that can trigger serotonin syndrome with SSRIs?
test.explain: Linezolid weakly but meaningfully inhibits MAO.

test.q: 5-HT2B agonism is linked to:
test.explain: Fenfluramine and pergolide caused valvulopathy this way.

test.q: Buspirone's anxiolytic effect is attributed to:
test.explain: Buspirone is not a benzodiazepine.

test.q: Pimavanserin is used for psychosis in Parkinson disease because it:
choices: Blocks D2 receptors strongly in the cortex
Is a 5-HT2A inverse agonist without D2 blockade
Inhibits MAO-B and raises dopamine levels
test.explain: Avoiding D2 blockade spares motor function.

test.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme in serotonin synthesis.
test.explain: TPH hydroxylates tryptophan to 5-HTP.

test.q: SSRIs block the serotonin transporter, abbreviated ___.
test.explain: SERT clears 5-HT from the synapse.

test.q: Name the 5-HT2A antagonist used as an antidote for serotonin syndrome.
test.explain: Cyproheptadine is an oral 5-HT2A and H1 antagonist.

test.q: The pineal gland converts serotonin into ___.
test.explain: Via N-acetylation and O-methylation.

kidTest.q: Where is most of your serotonin?
kidTest.explain: About 9 out of 10 parts are in the gut.

kidTest.q: Serotonin in the brain helps with:
kidTest.explain: It is a brain messenger for mood, sleep and more.

kidTest.q: Ondansetron is a medicine that stops:
kidTest.explain: It blocks a serotonin lock that triggers vomiting.

kidTest.q: Too much serotonin can make a person:
kidTest.explain: That is serotonin syndrome.

kidTest.q: Receptors are like ___ that serotonin can open.
kidTest.explain: Each receptor is a lock; drugs are keys.

kidTest.q: How many kinds of serotonin locks are there?
kidTest.explain: There are at least 14 subtypes.

advancedTest.q: Why do SSRIs take weeks to work, in the classic autoreceptor model?
choices: SSRIs need several weeks to be absorbed fully from the gut and reach the brain
SERT has to be resynthesized before serotonin reuptake can change
5-HT3 ion channels must slowly open before mood starts to improve
Raphe 5-HT1A autoreceptors initially reduce firing and must desensitize first
advancedTest.explain: Autoreceptor desensitization allows sustained terminal 5-HT increase.

advancedTest.q: A patient on sertraline receives methylene blue for vasoplegia and becomes agitated, febrile and clonic. Best explanation:
choices: Methylene blue blocks 5-HT3, causing serotonin rebound
Anaphylaxis to the blue dye given during the surgery
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome triggered by the dye
Methylene blue inhibits MAO-A, producing serotonin toxicity
advancedTest.explain: This interaction carries an FDA warning.

advancedTest.q: Why can telotristat ethyl treat carcinoid diarrhea without psychiatric effects?
choices: It blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the brain but not in the gut wall
It is a SERT inhibitor that keeps serotonin inside platelets
It degrades serotonin in the liver, which the brain doesn't use
It inhibits peripheral TPH and 5-HT does not cross the blood–brain barrier
advancedTest.explain: Peripheral and central pools are separate.

advancedTest.q: Why do antipyretics fail in severe serotonin toxicity?
choices: They are rapidly destroyed by MAO before reaching the brain
The heat comes from muscle activity, not a hypothalamic set-point change
They block sweating and other cooling mechanisms in the skin
The temperature rise is primarily due to infection rather than muscle activity
advancedTest.explain: Treatment is sedation, cooling and sometimes paralysis.

lessons.title: Ergots and Triptans

levels.kid:
A **migraine** is a very bad headache. It can throb, make light feel too bright, and make you feel sick to your stomach.

Long ago people found a fungus that grows on rye grain, called **ergot**. Eating moldy bread with it made people very sick: their fingers and toes could lose blood and turn black. But in tiny, careful amounts, chemicals from ergot became medicines that squeeze blood vessels and help migraines.

Later, scientists made a smarter key called a **triptan**. Triptans fit special serotonin locks near the nerves of the head. They calm those nerves and stop the migraine.

Because triptans also squeeze blood vessels, people with heart problems usually can't take them.
levels.hs:
**Ergot alkaloids** come from *Claviceps purpurea*, a fungus on rye. In the Middle Ages, contaminated bread caused **ergotism** ("St. Anthony's fire"): burning limbs, gangrene from intense vasoconstriction, and convulsions.

Ergot drugs bind many receptors (serotonin, α-adrenergic and dopamine), so they have many uses:
- **Ergotamine** and **dihydroergotamine (DHE)**: migraine.
- **Methylergonovine**: contracts the uterus to stop bleeding after childbirth.
- **Bromocriptine** and **cabergoline**: dopamine agonists that shrink **prolactin-secreting pituitary tumors**.

**Triptans** (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan) are selective **5-HT1B/1D agonists**:
- 5-HT1B on cranial blood vessels: constricts dilated vessels.
- 5-HT1D on trigeminal nerve endings: blocks release of pain-causing peptides like **CGRP**.

They work best taken early in an attack. Side effects include tingling and chest tightness. They are **not** for people with coronary artery disease, past stroke or uncontrolled high blood pressure. Don't combine ergots and triptans close together.

Newer migraine drugs avoid vasoconstriction:
- **Lasmiditan** (5-HT1F agonist).
- **Gepants** (ubrogepant, rimegepant): block the CGRP receptor.
- **CGRP antibodies** (erenumab, fremanezumab) for prevention.

Using any acute migraine drug too often can cause **medication-overuse headache**.
levels.college:
**Ergot pharmacology** is promiscuous partial agonism at 5-HT1, 5-HT2, α-adrenergic and dopamine receptors.
- **Ergotamine**: potent, long-lasting arterial vasoconstriction; nausea is common.
- **DHE**: more venoconstrictor than arterial, more α-antagonist; available IV, intranasal and injectable; used for status migrainosus and medication-overuse withdrawal.
- **Methylergonovine**: uterotonic for postpartum hemorrhage; contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia.
- **Bromocriptine, cabergoline**: D2 agonists for prolactinomas and acromegaly. Cabergoline is longer-acting and better tolerated, and is first-line for prolactinomas.
- **Methysergide** (largely withdrawn) caused retroperitoneal, pleural and valvular fibrosis.

**Ergot contraindications**: coronary or peripheral vascular disease, pregnancy, and strong **CYP3A4 inhibitors** (macrolides, HIV protease inhibitors, azole antifungals), which cause acute ergotism with limb ischemia.

**Triptans** are 5-HT1B/1D agonists. Their antimigraine effect comes from three sites: constriction of dilated meningeal vessels (1B), inhibition of CGRP and substance P release from trigeminal terminals (1D), and inhibition of second-order neurons in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis. They differ mainly in pharmacokinetics: sumatriptan has low oral bioavailability but works fastest subcutaneously (cluster headache); naratriptan and frovatriptan are slow and long (lower recurrence). Sumatriptan, rizatriptan and zolmitriptan are metabolized by **MAO-A**, so MAOIs are contraindicated; propranolol raises rizatriptan levels.

**Contraindications**: ischemic heart disease, prior stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura, and use within 24 hours of an ergot or another triptan.

**Non-vasoconstrictor alternatives**:
- **Lasmiditan** (5-HT1F, a "ditan"): CNS-penetrant, causes dizziness and sedation, carries a driving restriction and is a controlled substance.
- **Gepants**: small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonists (acute and preventive).
- **Monoclonal antibodies**: erenumab targets the receptor; fremanezumab, galcanezumab and eptinezumab target the ligand.
levels.phd:
**From vascular to neural theory.** Wolff's vascular hypothesis held that migraine pain reflects meningeal vasodilation, which made ergot vasoconstriction an obvious remedy. The triptan program at Glaxo (Humphrey) was explicitly designed around selective cranial vasoconstriction via the receptor then called "5-HT1-like". Yet later evidence decoupled pain from vessel caliber: dilation is neither necessary nor sufficient, and lasmiditan, which has no vasoconstrictor activity, aborts attacks. The modern framing is trigeminovascular: activation of trigeminal afferents releases **CGRP**, which sensitizes peripheral and central nociceptive pathways, with the brainstem and hypothalamus shaping attack timing.

**CGRP as a validated target.** CGRP rises in jugular venous blood during attacks and normalizes after triptans. CGRP infusion triggers migraine-like attacks in patients with migraine. The CGRP receptor is a heteromer of calcitonin-like receptor and RAMP1. Early gepants (telcagepant) showed efficacy but hepatotoxicity, which was compound-specific; later gepants avoided it. Antibodies, too large to cross the blood–brain barrier efficiently, still work, implying that a substantial component of the mechanism sits outside the barrier, at the trigeminal ganglion or dura.

**Ergot receptor promiscuity as structure.** The ergoline scaffold mimics the shared pharmacophore of serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine: an indole-like aromatic system and a basic nitrogen at a fixed distance. This explains both efficacy and toxicity, including 5-HT2B-mediated valvulopathy with pergolide and high cumulative cabergoline exposure in Parkinson disease.

**Triptans and 5-HT1B in coronary arteries.** Human coronary arteries express 5-HT1B, and triptans produce small coronary constriction in vitro. Chest symptoms in most patients are not ischemic, but the contraindication stands because a narrowed vessel has no reserve.

**Medication-overuse headache** reflects central sensitization and altered descending modulation with frequent acute-drug exposure; triptans induce it after fewer days per month than simple analgesics.
levels.expert:
**Before treating a "migraine," exclude the dangerous headache.** A thunderclap onset, worst-ever headache, new headache over age 50, focal deficits, papilledema, fever or neck stiffness needs imaging and sometimes lumbar puncture. Giving a triptan for undiagnosed **subarachnoid hemorrhage** or **reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS)** is a real error: RCVS is linked to vasoactive drugs including triptans, ergots and SSRIs, and causes recurrent thunderclap headaches, segmental vasoconstriction, convexity SAH and sometimes stroke. Pain relief after a triptan does not rule out SAH.

**Cluster headache**: subcutaneous sumatriptan and high-flow oxygen abort attacks; verapamil is the usual preventive (with ECG monitoring), and a short steroid bridge can be used.

**Status migrainosus** in the emergency department: dopamine antagonists (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide) with diphenhydramine to prevent akathisia, IV fluids, ketorolac, and DHE when there is no vascular contraindication. Avoid opioids: they worsen outcomes and medication overuse.

**Prolactinomas are the neurosurgical pituitary tumor treated with drugs first.** Cabergoline normalizes prolactin and shrinks most macroadenomas, often restoring vision from chiasmal compression without surgery. Pitfalls:
- Rapid shrinkage of an invasive tumor can open a skull-base defect and cause **CSF rhinorrhea**.
- Pituitary apoplexy can rarely occur.
- Impulse-control disorders can emerge with dopamine agonists; ask about them.
- Echocardiographic surveillance is considered with high cumulative exposure.
Surgery is reserved for intolerance, resistance, apoplexy or patient preference.

**Postpartum hemorrhage**: methylergonovine is avoided in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy because severe hypertension and stroke can result.

**Drug interactions to say out loud**: ergots with clarithromycin or ritonavir, and sumatriptan or rizatriptan with an MAOI.

keyPoints: Ergots: promiscuous 5-HT/α/DA ligands; ergotism = gangrene + convulsions; CYP3A4 inhibitors precipitate it
Methylergonovine: postpartum hemorrhage; bromocriptine/cabergoline: D2 agonists, cabergoline first-line for prolactinoma
Triptans: 5-HT1B (vessel) + 5-HT1D (trigeminal CGRP release) agonists; contraindicated in CAD, stroke, uncontrolled HTN
No triptan within 24 h of an ergot; MAOIs contraindicated with sumatriptan/rizatriptan/zolmitriptan
Lasmiditan (5-HT1F) and gepants/anti-CGRP antibodies treat migraine without vasoconstriction
Thunderclap headache: exclude SAH and RCVS before a triptan

examples.src: Patient on ritonavir takes ergotamine → cold, painful legs

examples.tr: Cabergoline first; surgery if resistant or intolerant

lessons.title: Eicosanoids and Prostaglandin Analogs

levels.kid:
The walls of your cells are made of fat. Hidden in that fat is a special piece called **arachidonic acid**.

When a cell gets hurt, it snips that piece out and turns it into tiny messengers called **prostaglandins**. They are like little shouts that say "Help! Something is wrong here!" They cause swelling, pain and fever.

But prostaglandins also do good jobs. They protect your stomach from its own acid, keep blood flowing in your kidneys, and help with having babies.

Doctors use copies of prostaglandins as medicines. One copy helps people with eye pressure problems. Another helps protect the stomach. Medicines like ibuprofen do the opposite: they stop prostaglandins being made, so pain and fever go down.
levels.hs:
**Eicosanoids** are 20-carbon signaling lipids made from **arachidonic acid**, which **phospholipase A2** releases from cell membranes.

Two main pathways:
- **Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)** makes **prostaglandins** and **thromboxane**.
- **Lipoxygenase** makes **leukotrienes** (next lesson).

Key prostanoids:
- **PGE2**: fever, pain, inflammation; protects the stomach; keeps kidney blood flow up.
- **PGI2 (prostacyclin)**: made by blood vessel walls; widens vessels and stops platelets sticking.
- **TXA2 (thromboxane)**: made by platelets; narrows vessels and makes platelets clump.
- **PGF2α**: contracts the uterus and airways.

Notice PGI2 and TXA2 are opposites. Their balance matters for clots.

**Prostaglandin drugs:**
- **Misoprostol** (PGE1 analog): protects the stomach in people taking NSAIDs; also used in obstetrics. Never for pregnant people for ulcer prevention, since it can cause miscarriage.
- **Latanoprost** (PGF2α analog) eye drops: lower eye pressure in **glaucoma**. Side effect: darker iris and longer eyelashes.
- **Alprostadil** (PGE1): keeps the ductus arteriosus open in newborns with certain heart defects until surgery.
- **Epoprostenol**, **treprostinil** (PGI2 analogs): treat **pulmonary arterial hypertension**.
- **Carboprost** (PGF2α analog) and **dinoprostone** (PGE2): obstetric uses.

**Corticosteroids** reduce eicosanoid production overall, and NSAIDs block COX.
levels.college:
**Synthesis.** Cytosolic **PLA2** (cPLA2α), activated by Ca2+ and MAP-kinase phosphorylation, releases arachidonic acid. **COX** (prostaglandin H synthase) has two activities: a cyclooxygenase site forming PGG2 and a peroxidase site reducing it to PGH2. Cell-specific terminal synthases determine output: platelets make TXA2 (thromboxane synthase); endothelium makes PGI2; mast cells make PGD2. **Glucocorticoids** suppress the pathway by inducing annexin A1 and repressing COX-2 and cPLA2 transcription.

**Receptors** are GPCRs: EP1 (Gq), EP2 and EP4 (Gs), EP3 (mostly Gi), IP (Gs), TP (Gq), FP (Gq), DP1 (Gs), DP2/CRTH2 (Gi, on Th2 cells and eosinophils).

**Physiology by organ:**
- **Fever**: cytokines induce COX-2 and mPGES-1 in brain endothelium; PGE2 acts on EP3 in the preoptic hypothalamus.
- **Pain**: PGE2 sensitizes nociceptors (EP receptors lower their threshold); it does not cause much pain alone.
- **Stomach**: PGE2/PGI2 increase mucus and bicarbonate, raise mucosal blood flow, and reduce acid (EP3 on parietal cells).
- **Kidney**: PGE2/PGI2 dilate the afferent arteriole when angiotensin II and sympathetic tone are high, maintaining GFR in heart failure, cirrhosis and volume depletion.
- **Ductus arteriosus**: PGE2 keeps it open in utero; NSAIDs (indomethacin, ibuprofen) close a persistent ductus in preterm infants; alprostadil keeps it open in ductal-dependent lesions (with apnea as a key adverse effect).
- **Uterus**: PGE2 and PGF2α ripen the cervix and contract myometrium.

**Analogs and key cautions:**
- Misoprostol: diarrhea; contraindicated in pregnancy for ulcer prophylaxis; uterine rupture risk with a prior uterine scar.
- Carboprost: bronchoconstriction through FP and TP, so avoid in asthma.
- Latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost: increase **uveoscleral outflow**; iris and periorbital pigmentation, eyelash growth.
- Epoprostenol: half-life of minutes, continuous IV infusion; interruption causes rebound pulmonary hypertension.
levels.phd:
**COX catalysis and the "peroxide tone."** The cyclooxygenase site requires activation by a lipid hydroperoxide that oxidizes the heme at the peroxidase site, generating a tyrosyl radical (Tyr385) that abstracts a hydrogen from arachidonic acid. The pathway's output therefore depends on cellular peroxide levels. This concept explains why acetaminophen inhibits prostaglandin synthesis in the brain (low peroxide) but poorly in inflamed tissue and platelets (high peroxide).

**COX-2 structure.** A single residue difference, valine 523 in COX-2 versus isoleucine in COX-1, opens a side pocket that coxibs exploit for selectivity. COX-2 also oxygenates endocannabinoids (2-AG, anandamide) into prostaglandin glycerol esters and ethanolamides, linking the two lipid systems.

**Beyond COX and LOX.**
- **Cytochrome P450 epoxygenases** form epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors, degraded by soluble epoxide hydrolase.
- **CYP4A/4F ω-hydroxylases** form **20-HETE**, a potent cerebral vasoconstrictor that inhibits BK channels in vascular smooth muscle. 20-HETE rises in CSF after subarachnoid hemorrhage and has been studied as a contributor to delayed cerebral ischemia.
- **Isoprostanes** form non-enzymatically by free-radical attack on membrane arachidonate; F2-isoprostanes are a reference biomarker of oxidative stress.

**Resolution of inflammation** is an active program. Lipid-mediator class switching produces **lipoxins** from arachidonate and **resolvins, protectins and maresins** from omega-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA). Aspirin-acetylated COX-2 makes 15R-HETE, converted to 15-epi-lipoxin A4 ("aspirin-triggered lipoxin"). This reframes inflammation resolution as something pharmacology can promote, not only block.

**The PGI2/TXA2 balance hypothesis** (FitzGerald) explained coxib cardiovascular risk: selective COX-2 blockade suppresses endothelial prostacyclin while platelet COX-1 thromboxane continues. Mouse IP-receptor knockouts showed accelerated thrombosis and atherogenesis, supporting the mechanism.
levels.expert:
**Prostanoid physiology at the bedside.**
- A patient with **heart failure or cirrhosis** given an NSAID develops oliguria: renal function was prostaglandin-dependent. The same logic underlies the "triple whammy" (ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic plus NSAID).
- **Glaucoma drops** are systemic drugs too: latanoprost can worsen uveitis and cystoid macular edema after cataract surgery; ask about eye drops in a medication history.
- **Pulmonary arterial hypertension** on IV epoprostenol: a pump failure or line occlusion is an emergency, because rebound pulmonary hypertension can cause right-heart collapse within minutes. Never stop the infusion to "simplify" a line during transport or surgery; keep a dedicated line.
- **Neonates**: alprostadil keeps a ductus open in ductal-dependent congenital heart disease until surgery; prepare for apnea.

**Obstetric hemorrhage algorithm** (uterotonics): oxytocin first, then methylergonovine (avoid in hypertension), carboprost (avoid in asthma), and misoprostol, alongside tranexamic acid and surgical measures. Knowing each drug's contraindication lets you choose in seconds.

**Neurosurgical relevance.**
- After **aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage**, the vasospasm window brings interest in vasoactive lipids including 20-HETE and the PGI2/TXA2 balance. Nimodipine (a calcium-channel blocker) remains the only drug with outcome benefit; other agents are investigational.
- Fever after brain injury worsens secondary injury, so antipyretics (acetaminophen, COX inhibitors) and surface cooling are used, recognizing that fever-control trials have not shown clear outcome benefit.
- Many surgeons avoid NSAIDs right after craniotomy over bleeding concerns, a debated practice; evidence is mixed.

**Glucocorticoids** suppress eicosanoids broadly, which is part of why dexamethasone reduces peritumoral vasogenic edema in brain tumors, alongside direct tightening of the blood–brain barrier. It does not help cytotoxic edema from stroke or head injury, and steroids worsened outcomes in traumatic brain injury (CRASH trial).

keyPoints: Arachidonic acid (from PLA2) → COX → PGH2 → PGE2, PGI2, TXA2, PGF2α, PGD2
PGI2 (endothelium): vasodilation, anti-platelet; TXA2 (platelets): vasoconstriction, aggregation
PGE2: fever (EP3 hypothalamus), pain sensitization, gastric protection, renal afferent dilation
Misoprostol (PGE1): NSAID ulcer prevention, obstetrics; latanoprost (PGF2α): glaucoma via uveoscleral outflow
Alprostadil keeps the ductus open; indomethacin/ibuprofen close it; epoprostenol/treprostinil for PAH
Carboprost avoided in asthma; glucocorticoids suppress PLA2/COX-2 pathways

examples.tr: Alprostadil keeps the ductus open; watch for apnea

lessons.title: Leukotrienes and Bradykinin

levels.kid:
Some messengers in your body make tubes squeeze and leak.

**Leukotrienes** are made from the same fat piece as prostaglandins. In people with asthma, they squeeze the air tubes in the lungs and fill them with sticky mucus. That makes breathing hard and wheezy. A pill called **montelukast** blocks them so the tubes stay more open.

**Bradykinin** is a tiny protein messenger. It makes blood vessels open wide and leak, so skin can puff up and feel sore.

Your body has a "cleaner" that chops up bradykinin. Some blood pressure pills block that cleaner by accident. Then bradykinin builds up and can cause a tickly **cough**, or rarely, big puffy swelling of the lips and tongue.
levels.hs:
**Leukotrienes** come from arachidonic acid through **5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX)**.
- **LTB4** calls in neutrophils (white blood cells).
- **LTC4, LTD4, LTE4** (the **cysteinyl leukotrienes**) cause strong airway constriction, mucus and leaky vessels. They are much more potent than histamine in the airway.

**Asthma drugs that target them:**
- **Montelukast** and **zafirlukast**: block the CysLT1 receptor. Montelukast has a boxed warning for mood and behavior changes, including suicidal thoughts and sleep problems.
- **Zileuton**: blocks 5-LOX; can injure the liver.

**Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease**: some people with asthma and nasal polyps get severe attacks after aspirin or other NSAIDs. Blocking COX shunts arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes.

**Bradykinin** is cut from kininogen by the enzyme **kallikrein**. It causes vasodilation, leaky vessels and pain.

It is broken down by **ACE** (angiotensin-converting enzyme) and **neprilysin**. So:
- **ACE inhibitors** (lisinopril, enalapril) can cause a dry **cough** and **angioedema** (deep swelling of lips, tongue and throat) because bradykinin builds up.
- **Sacubitril** (in sacubitril/valsartan) blocks neprilysin and also raises angioedema risk.

**Hereditary angioedema** comes from too little C1 inhibitor, so kallikrein runs wild. It is treated with bradykinin- or kallikrein-blocking drugs, not with antihistamines.
levels.college:
**Leukotriene synthesis.** On cell activation, 5-LOX translocates to the nuclear envelope, where **FLAP** (5-LOX-activating protein) presents arachidonic acid. 5-LOX forms LTA4, which is hydrolyzed to **LTB4** (BLT1 receptor: neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion) or conjugated with glutathione by LTC4 synthase to **LTC4**, then cleaved to LTD4 and LTE4. Together these cysteinyl leukotrienes were the "slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis." **CysLT1** mediates bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, edema and eosinophil recruitment.

**Leukotriene modifiers:**
- **Montelukast, zafirlukast**: CysLT1 antagonists; oral alternatives or add-ons in mild persistent asthma, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, allergic rhinitis and AERD. Less effective than inhaled corticosteroids. Zafirlukast inhibits CYP2C9 (raising warfarin effect) and is hepatotoxic. Montelukast's boxed warning (2020) covers neuropsychiatric events.
- **Zileuton**: 5-LOX inhibitor blocking both LTB4 and cysteinyl LTs; monitor liver enzymes; CYP1A2 inhibition raises theophylline.

**AERD (Samter's triad)**: asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and reactions to COX-1 inhibitors. COX-1 inhibition removes PGE2's brake on 5-LOX and mast cells, causing a cysteinyl leukotriene surge. Leukotriene modifiers help, and supervised aspirin desensitization followed by maintenance aspirin reduces polyp recurrence. Selective COX-2 inhibitors are generally tolerated.

**Kinin system.** Plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to bradykinin. **B2 receptors** (constitutive, Gq) mediate vasodilation via NO and PGI2, permeability and pain; **B1 receptors** are induced by inflammation. Bradykinin is degraded by **ACE (kininase II)**, neprilysin, aminopeptidase P and carboxypeptidase N.

**Bradykinin-mediated angioedema** lacks urticaria and itch, evolves over hours, can involve the bowel, and responds poorly to epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids. Causes: ACE inhibitors (more common in Black patients), neprilysin inhibition, combined ACE inhibitor with DPP-4 or mTOR inhibitors, hereditary or acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency. Targeted drugs: **icatibant** (B2 antagonist), **ecallantide** and **lanadelumab** (kallikrein inhibitors), **berotralstat** (oral kallikrein inhibitor), and **C1-inhibitor concentrate**. Sacubitril/valsartan must not be started until 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose.
levels.phd:
**Compartmentalization of leukotriene synthesis.** 5-LOX activity depends on Ca2+-dependent membrane binding, phosphorylation and FLAP, an integral nuclear-membrane protein of the MAPEG family (shared with LTC4 synthase and mPGES-1). FLAP inhibitors (MK-886 and successors) block leukotriene synthesis without touching 5-LOX itself and have been explored for asthma and atherosclerosis. **Transcellular biosynthesis** is the rule: neutrophils export LTA4 that platelets or endothelial cells, which lack 5-LOX, convert to LTC4 or lipoxins. Output is therefore an emergent property of cell mixtures.

**CysLT receptor heterogeneity.** LTE4 is a weak CysLT1 agonist but the dominant urinary metabolite and a potent inducer of airway eosinophilia in AERD, implicating other receptors (CysLT3/GPR99, P2Y12-dependent responses on platelets). Urinary LTE4 is a biomarker that rises after aspirin challenge in AERD. This incomplete coverage helps explain the modest efficacy of CysLT1 antagonists.

**Montelukast neuropsychiatric signal.** Montelukast penetrates the CNS, and CysLT1 and GPR17 receptors are expressed in brain. Pharmacovigilance and case-control data linked it to agitation, nightmares, depression and suicidality, prompting the 2020 boxed warning; the mechanism remains unproven.

**Bradykinin, ACE and the cough.** ACE has two catalytic domains; bradykinin is hydrolyzed efficiently by both. ACE inhibition increases bradykinin and substance P in airway tissue, sensitizing C-fibers via B2 and TRPV1/TRPA1 pathways, possibly with prostaglandin amplification, which is why ARBs, which do not affect kinin breakdown, rarely cause cough.

**Contact system and fibrinolysis.** Factor XII activation on negatively charged surfaces activates prekallikrein. Plasmin can also activate factor XII and generate bradykinin. This links thrombolysis to angioedema mechanistically and explains why C1-inhibitor, which inhibits factor XIIa, kallikrein and C1r/C1s, is the master regulator, and why its deficiency produces attacks.
levels.expert:
**Stroke unit pearl: alteplase angioedema.** Orolingual angioedema occurs in a small percentage of patients after IV thrombolysis, more often with ACE inhibitor use and with infarcts involving the insular and frontal cortex, and is often contralateral to the infarct. Plasmin generates bradykinin and ACE inhibition prevents its breakdown. Management: stop the infusion, give antihistamine and steroid (in case of a histaminergic component), escalate to icatibant, C1-inhibitor or fresh frozen plasma for progression, and secure the airway early, ideally awake fiberoptic intubation.

**Angioedema triage in the emergency department:**
- **With hives and itch, minutes after exposure**: histaminergic or anaphylactic; epinephrine works.
- **Without hives, slow over hours, on an ACE inhibitor**: bradykinin-mediated; epinephrine and antihistamines are often given but are unreliable; watch the airway, consider icatibant or FFP (evidence mixed), and stop the ACE inhibitor permanently. ARB switching carries a small cross-risk but is usually acceptable.
- **Recurrent abdominal pain and swelling with a family history**: hereditary angioedema; check C4 (low between attacks) and C1-inhibitor level and function.
Before elective surgery or dental work in hereditary angioedema, short-term prophylaxis with C1-inhibitor concentrate is standard, because intubation trauma triggers attacks.

**ACE inhibitor cough** can start weeks to months after initiation and resolves within weeks of stopping. Don't treat it with cough syrup; switch to an ARB.

**Asthma in practice.** A teenager on montelukast with new nightmares, low mood or suicidal thoughts should have the drug reviewed immediately; inhaled corticosteroid-based therapy is preferred. In AERD, nasal polyp surgery is often combined with aspirin desensitization afterward; biologics against IL-4Rα (dupilumab) reduce polyps.

**Perioperative**: NSAIDs for pain in a patient with nasal polyps and asthma can provoke severe bronchospasm; ask about past reactions, and choose acetaminophen or a COX-2 selective agent when appropriate.

keyPoints: 5-LOX + FLAP → LTA4 → LTB4 (neutrophil chemotaxis) or cysteinyl LTs C4/D4/E4 (bronchoconstriction, mucus, edema)
Montelukast/zafirlukast block CysLT1 (montelukast boxed warning: neuropsychiatric); zileuton inhibits 5-LOX (hepatotoxic)
AERD: asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID reactions; COX-1 block shunts to leukotrienes
Bradykinin from kininogen via kallikrein; B2 receptor; degraded by ACE and neprilysin
ACE inhibitors → cough and angioedema; sacubitril adds risk (36-hour washout from ACE inhibitor)
Bradykinin angioedema: no hives, poor epinephrine response; icatibant, kallikrein inhibitors, C1-INH

test.q: Which enzyme starts leukotriene synthesis from arachidonic acid?
test.explain: 5-LOX with FLAP forms LTA4.

test.q: Montelukast works by:
test.explain: It is a cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonist.

test.q: Zileuton requires monitoring of:
test.explain: Zileuton can cause hepatotoxicity.

test.q: Leukotriene B4 mainly:
test.explain: LTB4 acts on BLT1 for chemotaxis.

test.q: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough because they:
test.explain: ACE is kininase II.

test.q: Which feature suggests bradykinin-mediated rather than histamine-mediated angioedema?
choices: Onset within minutes of a bee sting
test.explain: Bradykinin angioedema lacks urticaria.

test.q: Icatibant works by:
test.explain: It is a B2 antagonist for hereditary angioedema attacks.

test.q: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease includes asthma, NSAID reactions and:
test.explain: Samter's triad.

test.q: Before starting sacubitril/valsartan, an ACE inhibitor must be stopped for at least:
test.explain: Combined neprilysin and ACE inhibition sharply raises angioedema risk.

test.q: Hereditary angioedema is caused by deficiency of which protein?
test.explain: Without it, kallikrein and factor XIIa activity go unchecked.

test.q: Bradykinin is released from kininogen by the enzyme ___.
test.explain: Kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen.

test.q: Which antihypertensive class rarely causes cough, making it the usual switch from an ACE inhibitor?
test.explain: ARBs do not inhibit kinin breakdown.

test.q: LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 are called the ___ leukotrienes.
test.explain: They contain a cysteine from glutathione.

kidTest.q: In asthma, leukotrienes make air tubes:
kidTest.explain: That makes breathing hard.

kidTest.q: Montelukast is a pill for:
kidTest.explain: It blocks leukotrienes.

kidTest.q: Bradykinin makes blood vessels:
kidTest.explain: Leaky vessels cause swelling.

kidTest.q: Some blood pressure pills can cause a tickly:
kidTest.explain: They let bradykinin build up.

kidTest.q: Big puffy swelling of the lips and tongue is called ___.
kidTest.explain: It can block the airway.

kidTest.q: Leukotrienes are made from the same fat piece as:
kidTest.explain: Both come from arachidonic acid.

advancedTest.q: Why are ACE inhibitor users at higher risk of angioedema after alteplase for stroke?
choices: Plasmin generates bradykinin and ACE inhibition blocks its breakdown
Alteplase blocks H1 receptors in the airway, releasing histamine instead
ACE inhibitors activate plasminogen, so the dose of alteplase is too high
Stroke releases leukotrienes, which ACE inhibitors fail to break down
advancedTest.explain: Two hits on the kinin pathway.

advancedTest.q: Why do CysLT1 antagonists only partly control AERD?
choices: LTE4 and other mediators act through receptors other than CysLT1
They are barely absorbed from the gut, so blood levels stay too low
They increase PGE2 production, which itself worsens AERD symptoms
They block COX-1 the way aspirin does, so they aggravate the disease
advancedTest.explain: LTE4 is a weak CysLT1 agonist but drives eosinophilia via other receptors.

advancedTest.q: Low C4 between attacks with recurrent non-itchy swelling and abdominal pain suggests:
choices: Allergic urticaria driven by mast cell IgE
advancedTest.explain: C1-INH deficiency allows ongoing C4 consumption.

advancedTest.q: Leukotriene production often requires transcellular biosynthesis because:
choices: Each cell type expresses the full enzyme set but just one releases leukotrienes
LTA4 is made mainly in the liver and travels in blood to inflamed tissue
Neutrophils export LTA4 that platelets or endothelium convert to LTC4
Platelets express 5-LOX and make LTA4, which neutrophils then convert
advancedTest.explain: Output depends on interactions among cell types.
